body: Harvey, Liu and Zhu, '... and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns' (Review of Financial Studies 29(1), 2016; ~2,200 Crossref citations) catalogued 316 factors published by 2012 and argued that the standard t > 2 threshold is meaningless when hundreds of researchers mine the same CRSP/Compustat data. Using multiple-testing corrections (Bonferroni, Holm, BHY), a newly proposed factor today should clear t > 3.0. Under their framework many historically 'significant' factors are likely false positives; they estimate a large share of claimed findings in finance are false. Harvey's later presidential address ('The Scientific Outlook in Financial Economics', JF 2017) adds p-hacking and publication bias warnings and recommends Bayesian 'minimum Bayes factor' reasoning. Replicated? It is a methods paper. JKP (2023) dispute how pessimistic it is but accept the logic. Use for us: this applies directly to our own backtests. Every time we test a screen on Indian data (for example 20 variants of a promoter-buying rule), we are multiple-testing. Rules: write the hypothesis and parameter choice down before testing; count every variant tried; demand t > 3 or an out-of-sample hold-out period (for example, build on 2005-2018 and test on 2019-2026); prefer signals with an economic story given in advance.
title: Harvey-Liu-Zhu (RFS 2016): after 300+ tested factors, a new one needs t > 3.0, not 2.0
